title: Designs for Learning: Studying Science Museum Exhibits That Do More Than Entertain

findings.antecedent: Bike Cycle exhibit (complex machine work schema, robot immediately recognizable, four large, color-coded buttons)
findings.consequent: visitor persistence until success
findings.mechanism: immediate apprehendability at the large scale (robot) and small scale (controls) reduces cognitive load, supporting intrinsic motivation to persist.
findings.quote: we found that 73% of visitors persisted until they had succeeded

findings.antecedent: Bike Cycle exhibit (complex machine work schema, robot immediately recognizable, four large, color-coded buttons)
findings.consequent: visitor satisfaction with challenge level
findings.mechanism: immediate apprehendability at the large scale (robot) and small scale (controls) allows visitors to engage with an appropriate level of challenge, leading to a 'flow' state.
findings.quote: and 70% said they thought the level of challenge was about right.

findings.antecedent: Downhill Race exhibit (competition/race schema, two side-by-side lanes, six disks with varying features)
findings.consequent: visitor predictions, explanations, and new understandings (articulated)
findings.mechanism: the familiar race schema provides a framework, freeing attention for visitors to think about disk characteristics and scientific principles.
findings.quote: several studies have shown that this exhibit provokes predictions, explanations, and new understandings that can be articulated

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit ('empty' tank of nocturnal frogs, 'watching and waiting' schema)
findings.consequent: visitor complex inferences (e.g., about camouflage, froggy lifestyle)
findings.mechanism: visitors recognized the exhibit as requiring waiting and watching, accepting the challenge and using it as an opportunity for deeper cognitive engagement.
findings.quote: this exhibit was the most likely of any in the exhibition to elicit complex inferences from visitors

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit ('empty' tank of nocturnal frogs, 'watching and waiting' schema)
findings.consequent: visitor stories and personal associations
findings.mechanism: the 'watching and waiting' framework encouraged visitors to share personal experiences and knowledge.
findings.quote: the second most likely element to evoke stories and personal associations

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit ('empty' tank of nocturnal frogs, 'watching and waiting' schema)
findings.consequent: visitor declarations of previous knowledge about frogs
findings.mechanism: the 'watching and waiting' framework encouraged visitors to share personal experiences and knowledge.
findings.quote: the second most likely to elicit declarations of previous knowledge about frogs.

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit ('empty' tank of nocturnal frogs, 'watching and waiting' schema)
findings.consequent: visitor expressed frustration or annoyance at having to look for frogs
findings.mechanism: visitors recognized the exhibit as an example of something where one had to wait and watch, accepting the challenge.
findings.quote: None of the 30 pairs of visitors expressed frustration or annoyance at having to look for the frogs

findings.antecedent: Detective puzzle schema used to frame the Whodunit exhibition (forensic science)
findings.consequent: visitor immediate apprehension of purpose and relationship of distinct elements (crime scene, DNA lab, autopsy lab)
findings.mechanism: familiar activity schema reduces cognitive load and provides a clear framework for understanding the exhibition's components.
findings.quote: allowed visitors to immediately apprehend the purpose and relationship of distinct elements

findings.antecedent: Highly interactive exhibit with live specimens (Glowing Worms, changeable lighting, focus, dish location) OR less interactive exhibit with live specimens (changeable lighting, focus)
findings.consequent: visitor holding time
findings.mechanism: having some form of interactivity with live animals was key for engagement.
findings.quote: visitors who saw one of the live, interactive versions of the exhibit stayed longer

findings.antecedent: Highly interactive exhibit with live specimens (Glowing Worms, changeable lighting, focus, dish location) OR less interactive exhibit with live specimens (changeable lighting, focus)
findings.consequent: visitor enjoyment rating
findings.mechanism: having some form of interactivity with live animals was key for enjoyment.
findings.quote: rated the exhibit as more enjoyable

findings.antecedent: Highly interactive exhibit with live specimens (Glowing Worms, changeable lighting, focus, dish location) OR less interactive exhibit with live specimens (changeable lighting, focus)
findings.consequent: visitor ability to reconstruct relevant details of experience
findings.mechanism: physical interaction with live specimens enhances memory encoding and recall.
findings.quote: able to reconstruct more relevant details of their experience

findings.antecedent: More interactive version of Glowing Worms exhibit (with changeable lighting, focus, dish location) vs. less interactive version (with changeable lighting, focus)
findings.consequent: visitor experience (holding time, enjoyment, recall)
findings.mechanism: more interactivity is not necessarily better; there may be an optimal degree of interactivity.
findings.quote: we found no significant differences between the experiences of visitors who used the more interactive version and those who used the less interactive version.

findings.antecedent: Exhibits containing live animals in glass terrariums (Frogs exhibition)
findings.consequent: attractiveness to visitors
findings.mechanism: innate human affiliation with nature and living things.
findings.quote: the exhibits containing live animals in glass terrariums were more attractive

findings.antecedent: Exhibits containing live animals in glass terrariums (Frogs exhibition)
findings.consequent: frequency and diversity of 'learning-talk' (conversations showing evidence of learning)
findings.mechanism: live animals stimulate more engagement and discussion among visitors.
findings.quote: evoked significantly more frequent and more diverse “learning-talk”

findings.antecedent: Videotape of frogs catching and eating their prey (single exhibit in Frogs exhibition)
findings.consequent: diversity of learning-talk
findings.mechanism: compelling visual content can drive deep cognitive engagement and discussion.
findings.quote: The single exhibit in the exhibition that evoked the greatest diversity of learning-talk

findings.antecedent: Videotape of frogs catching and eating their prey (single exhibit in Frogs exhibition)
findings.consequent: visitor holding times
findings.mechanism: compelling visual content can sustain visitor attention and engagement.
findings.quote: as well as the longest holding times

findings.antecedent: Active Prolonged Engagement (APE) exhibits (e.g., electrical circuit construction, freezing ice sheet)
findings.consequent: visitor holding time
findings.mechanism: APE exhibits support multiple simultaneous users and elicit self-generated explorations, leading to sustained engagement.
findings.quote: APE exhibits engaged visitors for more than twice as long as traditional exhibits.

findings.antecedent: Active Prolonged Engagement (APE) exhibits
findings.consequent: variety of 'driving questions' (initial thoughts upon approaching exhibit)
findings.mechanism: APE exhibits encourage diverse forms of inquiry and exploration, leading to a wider range of initial questions.
findings.quote: they elicited a broader variety of “driving questions,” defined as the initial thought that visitors had as they approached the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Active Prolonged Engagement (APE) exhibits
findings.consequent: variety in pattern and sequence of visitor physical interactions
findings.mechanism: APE exhibits elicit more self-generated explorations, leading to less constrained and more varied physical interactions.
findings.quote: visitors' physical interactions with APE exhibits varied in both pattern and sequence more than with the traditional exhibits

findings.antecedent: Downhill Race exhibit used with wooden disks specially designed to heighten salience of mass distribution
findings.consequent: visitor success in figuring out correct principle behind disks' behavior
findings.mechanism: making the key variable more salient reduces cognitive load and directs attention to the relevant scientific principle.
findings.quote: more visitors succeeded in figuring out the correct principle behind the disks' behavior.

findings.antecedent: Downhill Race exhibit used with wooden disks specially designed to heighten salience of mass distribution
findings.consequent: overall visitor holding time
findings.mechanism: by making the principle too obvious, it may reduce the opportunity for sustained inquiry and exploration.
findings.quote: the overall holding time decreased

findings.antecedent: Downhill Race exhibit used with wooden disks specially designed to heighten salience of mass distribution
findings.consequent: number of visitors who engaged deeply with the exhibit after reading the principle in the label
findings.mechanism: by making the principle too obvious, it may reduce the opportunity for sustained inquiry and exploration.
findings.quote: fewer visitors who could read the principle in the label engaged deeply with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Traditional exhibit label (invitation to interact + explanation of underlying principle) for Downhill Race exhibit
findings.consequent: number of visitors articulating the correct principle
findings.mechanism: direct explanation in the label facilitates understanding of the scientific principle.
findings.quote: resulted in more visitors articulating the correct principle

findings.antecedent: Traditional exhibit label (invitation to interact + explanation of underlying principle) for Downhill Race exhibit
findings.consequent: visitor deep engagement with the exhibit
findings.mechanism: providing the explanation upfront may reduce the motivation for self-directed inquiry and deep engagement.
findings.quote: led them to be less deeply engaged with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Addition of simple partitions around a group of related exhibits
findings.consequent: percentage of visitors correctly identifying common theme
findings.mechanism: partitions reduce distracting stimuli and help focus attention on the thematic connections, reducing cognitive overload.
findings.quote: increased the percentage of visitors who correctly identified their common theme from 30 to 51%

findings.antecedent: New Seeing Collection (designed for eye/brain function and cultural effects on seeing) vs. original Optics collection
findings.consequent: number of visitors talking about seeing as interpretation
findings.mechanism: explicit design for deeper conceptual insights into perception fosters more sophisticated discussions.
findings.quote: significantly more visitors to Seeing talked about seeing as interpretation

findings.antecedent: New Seeing Collection (designed for eye/brain function and cultural effects on seeing) vs. original Optics collection
findings.consequent: number of visitors mentioning specific parts of the visual system
findings.mechanism: explicit design for deeper conceptual insights into perception fosters more specific knowledge acquisition.
findings.quote: mentioned specific parts of the visual system

findings.antecedent: New Seeing Collection (designed for eye/brain function and cultural effects on seeing) vs. original Optics collection
findings.consequent: number of visitors expressing new appreciation for importance of attention in seeing
findings.mechanism: explicit design for deeper conceptual insights into perception fosters metacognitive awareness.
findings.quote: said they had a new appreciation of the importance of attention in seeing

findings.antecedent: New Seeing Collection (designed for eye/brain function and cultural effects on seeing) vs. original Optics collection
findings.consequent: number of visitors realizing people see things differently
findings.mechanism: explicit design for deeper conceptual insights into perception fosters perspective-taking and conceptual change.
findings.quote: said they hadn't realized that people see things differently

findings.antecedent: New Seeing Collection (designed for eye/brain function and cultural effects on seeing) vs. original Optics collection
findings.consequent: number of visitors finding exhibits related to their daily lives
findings.mechanism: explicit design for deeper conceptual insights into perception fosters personal relevance and meaning-making.
findings.quote: found that the exhibits related to their daily lives.

findings.antecedent: Traits of Life collection (exhibition strategy displaying diverse living creatures to illustrate commonalities)
findings.consequent: communication of abstract theme ('four characteristics common to all living things')
findings.mechanism: visitors interpreted the display as diversity rather than commonalities, indicating difficulty in conceptual change and preference for existing schemas.
findings.quote: Traits of Life collection was less successful in communicating its abstract theme

findings.antecedent: Temporary exhibition environment
findings.consequent: visitor explicit connections among exhibits
findings.mechanism: visitors may not expect to look for strong inter-exhibit links in an open environment, leading to low rates of explicit connection-making.
findings.quote: visitors made explicit connections among exhibits at only 5% of the exhibits at which they stopped.

findings.antecedent: Multisensory additions (objects for touching, listening, smelling, activity stations) to traditional dioramas (Boston Museum of Science)
findings.consequent: overall visitor experience
findings.mechanism: appealing to diverse learning styles and sensory modes enhances engagement and accessibility for all visitors.
findings.quote: the changes improved the experience for visitors in general

findings.antecedent: Multisensory additions (objects for touching, listening, smelling, activity stations) to traditional dioramas (Boston Museum of Science)
findings.consequent: visitor holding time
findings.mechanism: increased sensory engagement and diverse activities sustain visitor attention.
findings.quote: dramatic increases in holding time

findings.antecedent: Multisensory additions (objects for touching, listening, smelling, activity stations) to traditional dioramas (Boston Museum of Science)
findings.consequent: visitor label use
findings.mechanism: increased engagement with the exhibit encourages visitors to seek more information from labels.
findings.quote: label use

findings.antecedent: Multisensory additions (objects for touching, listening, smelling, activity stations) to traditional dioramas (Boston Museum of Science)
findings.consequent: visitor understanding of the area's major themes
findings.mechanism: diverse modes of interaction and information presentation facilitate deeper conceptual understanding.
findings.quote: understanding of the area's major themes.

findings.antecedent: Exhibit collections that are quieter, carpeted, with selective lighting and partitioning of space, supporting observation and reflection
findings.consequent: visitor notice and value of diversity of spaces within the museum
findings.mechanism: these environments provide opportunities for cognitive restoration and focused reflection, which visitors appreciate as a contrast to high-energy areas.
findings.quote: visitors notice and value the diversity of such spaces within the museum

findings.antecedent: Inquiry video clips (asking short questions inviting further exploration) added to existing exhibits
findings.consequent: visitor preference
findings.mechanism: inquiry-based prompts align with visitors' intrinsic motivation for exploration and cognitive engagement.
findings.quote: inquiry videos were preferred by visitors

findings.antecedent: Inquiry video clips (asking short questions inviting further exploration) added to existing exhibits
findings.consequent: visitor integration of exhibit experience into prior knowledge
findings.mechanism: inquiry prompts encourage active processing and connection-making with existing schemas.
findings.quote: helped them integrate the exhibit experience into their prior knowledge

findings.antecedent: Narrative video clips (four different people tell personal story about connection to exhibit) added to existing exhibits
findings.consequent: impact on learning or personal connections
findings.mechanism: narratives were often too loosely associated or metaphorical, and the noisy environment was not conducive to listening.
findings.quote: narratives showed little or no impact compared with the control condition.

findings.antecedent: Narrative video clip in the form of an unfolding drama with young children (added to existing exhibits)
findings.consequent: evoking personal connections in visitors' lives
findings.mechanism: a dramatic, relatable narrative with human characters can resonate more deeply with visitors.
findings.quote: this showed some evidence of evoking personal connections in more visitors' lives

stimuli.description: Water Standing on Air exhibit (plexiglass cylinder, metal mesh, water)

Bike Cycle exhibit (robotic simulation of bicycle rider with hydraulic pistons and control buttons)

Whodunit exhibition (crime scene, DNA lab, simulated autopsy laboratory)

Videotape of frogs catching and eating their prey

Simple partitions around a group of related exhibits
Seeing Collection exhibits (replacing original Light, Vision, Color, and Optics collection)

Boston Museum of Science dioramas with multisensory additions (objects for touching, listening, smelling, activity stations)

limitations: Need to know more about the impacts of apprehendability versus challenge, and the way in which the tension between them plays out at different scales in the museum visit, at different times, and with different audiences.
Need for further study of the impact of interactivity on learning.
Field badly needs more studies of nonverbal forms of learning because these may be the dominant forms for a three-dimensional physical interaction, especially for children.

Nonverbal studies would also help to reveal the learning impacts of a controversial and increasingly common display technique we call “gratuitous interactivity,” where the interactive features of an exhibit are unrelated to its central phenomenon.
Large-scale design issues (e.g., conceptual coherence) are logistically difficult and expensive to test in real museum settings.
How can we encourage visitors to make more connections among exhibits in a collection?
What are realistic abstractions in relation to visitors' prior knowledge?
To what extent can the abstract concepts and themes of science be framed and embodied to provide context and significance for an otherwise fragmented experience?

More research is needed to determine whether instantiations of narrative have simply been flawed, or whether perhaps the chaotic, high-energy environment of a science museum and the nonanecdotal nature of science combine to make storytelling an ineffective strategy for learning in these settings.
